title: Amortised inference throughone-step implicit sampling

paper.title: Amortised inference through one-step implicit sampling
paper.abstract:
Abstract Efficient sampling from Bayesian posterior distributions in high dimensions remains a hard problem, despite advances in theory and algorithms.
Multiple steps are usually required to draw unbiased samples, for example, iterations of an MCMC algorithm or integration steps in a diffusion-based amortised sampler.
However, scalable one-step amortised inference remains a challenging open problem.
In this work, we build upon recent progress in data-driven generative modelling to offer a possible solution for one-step amortised sampling.
Our one-step implicit sampler ( OSIS ) uses short-time MCMC dynamics to define a local target for the evolution of an implicitly modelled distribution.
In the asymptotic limit, the modelled distribution is a fixed point of the MCMC kernel and thus samples from the target.
We analyse the convergence properties of OSIS and show connections with other generative modelling and sampling algorithms.
We study various design choices and show that OSIS performs well compared to multi-step amortised samplers
and non-amortised MCMC baselines while being far more efficient at sampling time.

sections.heading: The sampling problem.
sections.text: Many problems in physics, biology, statistics, and machine learning ( Welling and Teh, 2011 ; Wirnsberger et al., 2020 ; Noé et al., 2019 ; Holdijk et al., 2023 ) require drawing samples from a distribution whose density is known up to a normalising constant. Formally, this means sampling from a distribution defined via an energy function ℰ : ℝ d → ℝ \mathcal{E}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} , with density π ⁡ ( x ) = e − ℰ ⁡ ( x ) / Z , Z = ∫ ℝ d e − ℰ ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x . \pi(x)={e^{-\mathcal{E}(x)}}/Z,\quad Z={\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\mathcal{E}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x}. (1) A typical instance of this problem is Bayesian inference: a posterior π ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) ∝ p ⁡ ( x ) ​ p ​ ( y ∣ x ) \pi(x\mid y)\propto p(x)p(y\mid x) over a variable x x given an observation y y has the form in ( 1 ) with ℰ ⁡ ( x ) = − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( x ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) \mathcal{E}(x)=-\log p(x)-\log p(y\mid x) . The classic way to sample from a distribution as in ( 1 ) is by using (training-free) Monte Carlo algorithms. Many such algorithms draw samples by simulating an ergodic chain using π \pi -invariant kernels for a sufficiently long time. Popular Monte Carlo algorithms include Metropolis-Hastings ( Metropolis et al., 1953 ; Hastings, 1970 ) , unadjusted and Metropolis-adjusted Langevin ( Rossky et al., 1978 ; Besag, 1994 ; Roberts and Tweedie, 1996 ) , Hamiltonian Monte Carlo ( Duane et al., 1987 ; Neal, 2011 ) , and sequential Monte Carlo ( Del Moral et al., 2006 ) . The use of these methods comes at the cost of running chains for many steps, or with many simulated particles, to obtain high-quality samples from the target. Generative modelling algorithms that learn to imitate unbiased samples from a distribution – i.e. , approximate an empirical measure – scale quite successfully, as evidenced by many large-scale applications of deep learning ( Kong et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) . Meanwhile, generative modelling algorithms that rely only on a density function, without unbiased samples, continue to lag behind, and scaling them remains a challenge despite the deep significance of this problem.

sections.heading: Amortised sampling.
sections.text: Deep learning has brought about new possibilities for introducing learnable components into sampling algorithms. Such components allow to spend more time and compute for training, yet gain speed when sampling and exploit generalisable structure in the target. Amortisation techniques include learning MCMC transition kernels ( Song et al., 2017 ; Samsonov et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , amortising MCMC dynamics ( Li et al., 2017 ) , and training density estimators to sample from unnormalised distributions ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Midgley et al., 2023 ) . The most successful family of amortised samplers adopts diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) as approximators of the target distribution ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ; Richter et al., 2024 ; Sendera et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2025 ; Berner et al., 2026 ; Havens et al., 2025 , e.g. ,) . Diffusion samplers introduce a learnable stochastic process to model the transition dynamics from a known distribution to a target, usually by approximately reversing a fixed noising process. In contrast to diffusion models trained using a variational bound on the likelihood of empirical samples, diffusion samplers are trained using stochastic optimal control objectives ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ; Berner et al., 2024 ) or path-space divergences ( Richter et al., 2020 ; Lahlou et al., 2023 ) , among other choices. Recent work has found and exploited connections between diffusion samplers and amortisation of SMC ( Choi et al., 2026 ) . sections.heading: One-step amortised sampling.
sections.text: Although diffusion samplers allow for a considerable inference speed-up by avoiding long-chain MCMC, they require simulation of a neural stochastic dynamical system during both training and sampling. Amortised sampling with a single neural function evaluation, however, remains a challenge. Although it is possible to use normalising flows for one-step sampling ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ) , they require the invertibility of a neural network and efficient computation of its Jacobian, both of which remain significant constraints. More recent work shows that such methods scale poorly and are prone to mode collapse ( He et al., 2025 ) . These methods can further be placed within a Monte Carlo outer loop and augmented with MCMC sampling ( Midgley et al., 2023 ) . In an attempt to design an efficient one-step sampler, we take a different approach, drawing inspiration from the novel paradigm in generative modelling termed drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ) . Drifting models evolve a implicit distribution towards an empirical target by defining a local direction for its evolution via a drifting field estimated from batches of target and generated samples. Such an approach, cannot be directly applied to sampling, as it requires access to samples from the target distribution to compute the drifting field.

sections.heading: Our contributions.
sections.text: We bypass this limitation by using an MCMC kernel invariant to the target distribution to implicitly define a drifting field. This leads us to the first main contribution: (1) We propose an algorithm for training a one-step implicit sampler ( OSIS ) using an objective that enforces invariance of the sampler’s output distribution to a target-invariant MCMC kernel ( Section 2.1 ). There have been prior attempts to design a one-step amortised sampling algorithm, using kernel density approximations to circumvent data unavailability ( Cao et al., 2026 ) and using adversarial training ( Li et al., 2017 ) . We discuss the connections between OSIS , drifting models, computational Wasserstein gradient flows, and this prior work in Section 3 . We also study the theoretical properties of OSIS , showing global convergence under assumptions similar to those in the MCMC literature: 1. We prove convergence of OSIS under asymptotic conditions and constraints on the target ( Section 4 ). To achieve scalability and efficiency in practice, we study the empirical performance of OSIS under different design choices, such as choice of MCMC kernel, empirical divergence, and other techniques: 1. We study design choices for OSIS ( § 5 ) and their influence on performance ( Table 3 ). Finally, we benchmark our sampler on amortised inference problems ranging from synthetic targets to posterior sampling under large-scale image model priors, leading to our final contribution: 1. We show that OSIS performs on par with multi-step baselines, while being more efficient ( § 6.1 ) and remaining scalable ( § 6.2 ).

sections.text: Suppose that K K is a stochastic kernel from ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} to ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} ( i.e. , a conditional distribution K ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) K(y\mid x) satisfying measurability conditions). sections.heading: Connection to other implicit samplers.
sections.text: The connection between generative modelling and implicit models, those without a parametrisation of density, goes back to Mohamed and Lakshminarayanan (2016) . Subsequent works explored algorithms that use MCMC to train implicit samplers: Feng et al. (2017) amortises Stein variational gradient descent ( Liu and Wang, 2016 , SVGD;) , while Titsias (2017) fits an invertible map to sample from the distribution induced by a short MCMC chain. Related approaches include Hoffman (2017) , Ruiz and Titsias (2019) , Gabrié et al. (2022) , and Yi and Liu (2023) . The closest precursor to OSIS is Li et al. (2017) . That algorithm initialises an MCMC chain from an implicit approximation network, applies a transition kernel, and updates the network with an adversarial loss matching the initial samples to their few-step refinements. OSIS differs from this line of work in three key ways. First, unlike Li et al. (2017) , OSIS does not rely on an adversarial loss, but remains stable with a fixed choice of empirical divergence. Second, OSIS is compatible with any MCMC kernel and any divergence between distributions, and we compare several choices of each (see Table 3 for kernels and Tables 1 and 1 for divergences). Third, we link the convergence of these methods to the convergence of the underlying MCMC kernel and establish a connection to Wasserstein gradient flows that was not known before in the sampling context (see Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Connection to drifting models.
sections.text: OSIS can be linked to drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , which define a local target for the evolution of a modelled distribution to guide it towards a target given empirically through data samples. Although OSIS and drifting models solve different problems (approximating an empirical data distribution and an energy-based distribution, respectively), they share some similarities. In Deng et al. (2026) , stationarity of an implicitly defined generative model is expressed through a drifting field, a vector field defining an evolution of particles under which the target distribution is stationary under asymptotic conditions. The field is defined similarly to the gradient of a kernel-based divergence and thus evolves model-generated samples towards the data distribution over the course of training. Unlike in diffusion and flow-based models, which approximate a time-dependent evolution, this field is a non-stationary training target, rather than part of the generation process. More recent works propose other ways to define this drifting field, some of which can be identified with gradients of divergences between distributions, making the training process simulate a gradient flow ( He et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . As we discuss below, OSIS shares parts of this connection; however, drifting models and their successors approximate the vector field giving the gradient flow , whereas OSIS uses the vector field giving the gradient flow to define the local target for optimisation . Cao et al. (2026) propose several ways to adapt drifting models for sampling. Their method relies on either Monte Carlo simulation or second-order derivatives to approximate the gradient of the energy, both of which scale poorly with dimensionality. In contrast, OSIS defines the drift implicitly by computing the divergence between two probability distributions.

In practice, this assumption is satisfied in the infinite-particle limit of empirical estimation of the divergence and with perfect numerical integration in the Monte Carlo updates. (2) We assume that optimisation of the modelled distribution is performed in Wasserstein space, rather than the parameter space ( θ \theta ). This can be achieved in practice by replacing the gradient step on 𝒲 2 2 \mathcal{W}_{2}^{2} with respect to θ \theta by a proximal gradient step in the 𝒲 2 2 \mathcal{W}_{2}^{2} geometry and assuming the parametric family and optimisation algorithm are sufficiently expressive to perform this step exactly. Our analysis uses that the evolution of density given by Langevin dynamics is the WGF of the KL divergence functional; we show that OSIS inherits the convergence properties of Langevin dynamics ( Durmus and Moulines, 2017 ; Chewi et al., 2025 , e.g. ,) .

sections.heading: 5 Practical considerations
sections.text: The idealised setting, which is detailed in Algorithm 1 and theoretically analysed in Section 4 cannot be implemented in practice. Instead, we approximate the distributions and the divergence between them 8by their empirical counterparts and replace the continuous-time Langevin by a discrete-time MCMC simulation. The next paragraphs detail various design choices for OSIS relevant in practice. An extended introduction to the practical considerations of the algorithm is provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Refinement kernel.
sections.text: OSIS can be instantiated with different MCMC kernels. The theory concerns exact Langevin, but we use the MALA kernel in practice and consider other choices in Table 3 .

sections.heading: Empirical divergence.
sections.text: It is not possible to use infinite populations as considered in the theory, instead OSIS computes finite-batch empirical divergences between generated samples and their kernel-refined versions. Our presented theory considers a squared 2-Wasserstein loss, but OSIS can be extended to other discrepancies between distributions. For the experiments on the synthetic targets ( Section 6.1 ) we use sliced Wasserstein distances ( Bonneel et al., 2015 , SWD;) , and for the experiments on Bayesian posteriors ( Section 6.2 ) we use minibatch OT with squared-Euclidean cost, which converges to exact 2-Wasserstein in the limit ( Fatras et al., 2021 ) .

sections.heading: Annealing.
sections.text: Kernel refinements can initially target the tempered distribution π β ∝ exp ⁡ ( − β ​ ℰ ) \pi_{\beta}\propto\exp(-\beta\mathcal{E}) with β t \beta_{t} and then anneal β \beta to 1 over the course of training. The starting temperature and annealing schedule balance early exploration with learning the final target.

sections.heading: Complete algorithm.
sections.text: To facilitate training stability, we make several gradient steps after each MCMC refinement. The complete training procedure detailing the use of empirical divergence, finite-step MCMC kernel, annealing, and multiple gradient steps per iteration is presented in Algorithm 3 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We evaluate OSIS against several amortised samplers: the normalising-flow-based FAB ( Midgley et al., 2023 ) and diffusion samplers trained with different algorithms – PIS ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ) , DIS ( Berner et al., 2024 ) , and off-policy methods TB + + MALA ( Sendera et al., 2024 ) and SubTB + + SMC ( Choi et al., 2026 ) . Since FAB can either be used as a one-step sampler or placed in an annealed importance sampling loop, we compare OSIS to the one-step version of FAB as well. sections.text: Table 1 shows sample-based metrics on synthetic targets, with 2-Wasserstein and MMD evaluated between 10000 draws from a trained OSIS model and an equal number of oracle samples from the target. OSIS is not consistently outperformed by any of the MCMC, normalising flow, or diffusion-based baselines despite requiring only one neural function evaluation and no energy evaluations to draw a sample. While the diffusion-based samplers trained by off-policy methods ( Sendera et al., 2024 ; Choi et al., 2026 ) are the strongest overall, they require many sampling steps to perform well, cf. the analysis in Berner et al. On the higher-dimensional targets – given by normalising flow densities trained on MNIST and FMNIST treated as energy-based models – OSIS again performs on par with FAB and stronger than diffusion-based samplers ( Table 2 ). It is clear from the figure that OSIS performs comparably in terms of sampling quality while being significantly faster at inference.

sections.text: The main advantage of one-step generative models is low sampling cost. OSIS , a one-step sampler, is much more efficient at sampling time than most baselines, whose sampling procedures require hundreds of function evaluations. sections.heading: Ablation of kernel choice.
sections.text: Table 3 compares different choices of the kernel in OSIS (see § C.1 for a description of the kernels). MALA, ULA, and OBABO tend to preform the strongest, and the higher-order splitting schemes for underdamped Langevin (OBABO and BAOAB) often improve over MALA, approaching the diffusion sampler baselines. However, based on the experiments, OSIS does not consistently benefit from sophisticated MCMC kernels. Additionally, we compare with the RWMH kernel, which does not use energy gradients. Although it does not provide the best performance, it remains competitive and can serve as an alternative when target-energy gradients are unavailable. Note that these methods are compared in terms of OSIS training steps, not at matched computational cost, and different kernels require different numbers of energy and gradient evaluations per step. Further ablations are provided in § E.4 .

sections.heading: 6.2 Bayesian posterior sampling under deep generative model priors
sections.text: We show the scalability of OSIS by applying it to the problem of sampling from a Bayesian posterior under a pretrained generative model prior in latent space, known otherwise as outsourced sampling ( Venkatraman et al., 2025 ) . Suppose that a pretrained generative model is expressed as a deterministic transformation of a latent variable: x = g ⁡ ( z ) x=g(z) , where z ∼ q ⁡ ( z ) z\sim q(z) follows a known base distribution. The model’s distribution over x x , p = g # ​ q p=g_{\#}q , is treated as a Bayesian prior. If r r is a likelihood or reward function, we wish to sample from the posterior, or reward-tilted distribution (which has density proportional to p ⁡ ( x ) ​ r ​ ( x ) p(x)r(x) if p p has a density). It can be shown that this posterior is the pushforward by g g of the latent-space distribution with density proportional to q ⁡ ( z ) ​ r ​ ( g ⁡ ( z ) ) q(z)r(g(z)) , reducing sampling from the posterior in x x -space to sampling from this distribution over the latent z z . sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper has proposed an algorithm for one-step amortised sampling based on matching the distribution induced by a generator with its MCMC refinement. With appropriate techniques to make the refinement and divergence optimisation practical, OSIS performs surprisingly well compared to strong samplers that require many neural net and energy evaluations to draw each sample. The most immediate challenge is to improve the sampling quality on highly multimodal targets, where diffusion samplers have been successful due to the geometric mixing induced by the noise, which is absent with tempering alone. The theoretical analysis should also be extended to include temperature annealing and inexact integration of the dynamics within various refinement kernels.

sections.heading: A.1 Vector-field-based loss
sections.text: It is possible to an consider alternative training procedure for OSIS , which is similar to the one used for drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ) . Gradient descent on the parameters θ \theta along the objective in ( 2 ) approximates the Wasserstein gradient descent of the distribution ρ \rho along the Wasserstein gradients of the divergence 𝒟 \mathcal{D} (see Section 3 ). The theory of Wasserstein geometry ( Ambrosio et al., 2005 ) tells us that the evolution of a distribution can be identified with the evolution of particles that follow this distribution along a gradient field. In this case, the evolution of particles follows a vector field V V such that V = − ∇ δ ​ 𝒟 δ ​ ρ θ V=-\nabla\frac{\delta\mathcal{D}}{\delta\rho_{\theta}} , with the term on the right being the gradient of the first variation of 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . This observation allows us to use an alternative training objective: ℒ ( θ ) = 𝔼 z ∼ q [ | | G θ ( z ) − sg [ G θ ( z ) + η V ( G θ ( z ) ) ] ‖ 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim q}\left[\left||G_{\theta}(z)-\text{sg}\left[G_{\theta}(z)+\eta V(G_{\theta}(z))\right]\right\|^{2}\right], (12) where now V V , rather than the divergence 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , is estimated empirically using samples from ρ θ \rho_{\theta} . The algorithm corresponding to this objective is presented in Algorithm 2 and experiments are in Section E.3 .

sections.heading: 2-Wasserstein distance.
sections.text: For distributions ρ , μ ∈ 𝒫 2 ​ ( ℝ d ) \rho,\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) , we define 2-Wasserstein distance as 𝒲 2 2 ​ ( ρ , μ ) = inf γ ∈ Γ ⁡ ( ρ , μ ) ∫ ℝ d × ℝ d | x − y | 2 ​ 𝑑 γ ​ ( x , y ) , \mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\rho,\mu)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}|x-y|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y), (15) where Γ ⁡ ( ρ , μ ) \Gamma(\rho,\mu) is the set of probability measures on ℝ d × ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} whose marginals are ρ \rho and μ \mu . ( 15 ) defines the Kantorovich version of OT. For measures in 𝒫 2 ​ ( ℝ d ) \mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) , the infimum is achieved ( i.e. , the minimal coupling exists) and the minimiser is unique. Moreover, for 𝒫 2 ​ ( ℝ d ) \mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) the optimal coupling has the form γ ∗ = ( Id , T ) # ​ ρ \gamma^{*}=(\operatorname{Id},T)_{\#}\rho for some T : ℝ d → ℝ d T:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} . This T T is the solution to the Monge OT problem, which appears in another (in this case, equivalent) definition of 2-Wasserstein distance: 𝒲 2 2 ( ρ , μ ) = inf T : T # ​ ρ = μ ∫ | T ( x ) − x | 2 ρ ( x ) d x . \mathcal{W}^{2}_{2}(\rho,\mu)=\inf_{T:T_{\#}\rho=\mu}\int|T(x)-x|^{2}\,\rho(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. In any of these definitions, 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} satisfies the triangle inequality, meaning that 2-Wasserstein is a distance metric in 𝒫 2 ​ ( ℝ d ) \mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) .

sections.heading: Appendix C Extended practical considerations
sections.text: This appendix details the main design choices of OSIS . It expands on the kernel, loss, tempering, and inference choices in § 5 . This section aims to provide a general overview. Specific details about the experiments are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: C.1 Choice of MCMC kernel
sections.text: We present here various methods to update the generated samples towards the target π \pi . They often consist of a π \pi -invariant MCMC kernel, but other methods, such as Stein variational gradient descent ( Liu and Wang, 2016 ) , can also be investigated. In this subsection, q ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) q(y\mid x) denotes a proposal density. We describe kernels for a fixed target π \pi . Under an annealing schedule, the same constructions use π β t \pi_{\beta_{t}} instead.

sections.heading: Metropolis-Hastings.
sections.text: The Metropolis-Hastings ( Metropolis et al., 1953 ; Hastings, 1970 , MH) kernel modifies a continuous full-support proposal to be π \pi -invariant by mixing it with a rejection kernel. To be precise, given a proposal kernel q q , define K ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) = α ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ q ​ ( y ∣ x ) + ( 1 − A ⁡ ( x ) ) ​ δ x ​ ( y ) , K(y\mid x)=\alpha(x,y)q(y\mid x)+(1-A(x))\delta_{x}(y), (20) where δ x \delta_{x} is a Dirac delta at x x and α ⁡ ( x , y ) = min ⁡ ( 1 , π ⁡ ( y ) ​ q ​ ( x ∣ y ) π ⁡ ( x ) ​ q ​ ( y ∣ x ) ) , A ⁡ ( x ) = ∫ α ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ q ​ ( y ∣ x ) ​ 𝑑 y . \alpha(x,y)=\min\left(1,\frac{\pi(y)q(x\mid y)}{\pi(x)q(y\mid x)}\right),\quad A(x)=\int\alpha(x,y)q(y\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}y. (21) By construction, K K is π \pi -invariant (in particular, if q q is reversible with respect to π \pi , then A ⁡ ( x ) = 1 A(x)=1 for π \pi -almost every x x and K = q K=q ). However, the choice of q q greatly affects the rate of convergence to π \pi of a Markov chain with transition operator K K .

sections.heading: Random-walk proposals.
sections.text: Random-walk Metropolis (RWM) is a commonly used form of MH. A standard variant takes q q to be the kenrel of a Gaussian randmo walk: q ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( y , x , σ 2 ​ I ) q(y\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(y;x,\sigma^{2}I) for some chosen variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} . The proposal is symmetric, so its acceptance probability simplifies to min ⁡ ( 1 , π ⁡ ( y ) / π ⁡ ( x ) ) \min(1,\pi(y)/\pi(x)) . RWM requires target energy evaluations but no target energy gradients.

sections.heading: Langevin-based proposals.
sections.text: One can make use of target gradient information when defining a proposal distribution. Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin ( Rossky et al., 1978 ; Besag, 1994 ; Roberts and Tweedie, 1996 , MALA;) is MH based on a proposal q q that is an Euler-Maruyama integration step of a Langevin SDE: q ( y ∣ x ) = 𝒩 ( y ; x − δ ∇ ℰ ( x ) , 2 δ I d ) q(y\mid x)=\mathcal{N}\left(y;x-\delta\nabla\mathcal{E}(x),2\delta I_{d}\right) for some chosen step size δ > 0 \delta>0 . At inverse temperature β t \beta_{t} , the drift becomes − δ β t ∇ ℰ ( x ) -\delta\beta_{t}\nabla\mathcal{E}(x) . Unlike RWM, this proposal is generally asymmetric, so both proposal-density terms in ( 21 ) must be retained. Omitting the accept/reject step gives the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA), which does not in general preserve the target at a finite step size ( Roberts and Tweedie, 1996 ) . Neither a MALA step nor a ULA step is the exact Langevin semigroup transition K h K^{h} used in § 4 .

sections.heading: Higher-order splitting schemes.
sections.text: Splitting integrators provide further discretisations of Langevin dynamics and can reduce finite-step sampling bias ( Leimkuhler and Matthews, 2013a ) . The idea is to divide the dynamics into simpler parts that can each be integrated exactly, then compose their updates. We consider the matrix formulation of the underdamped Langevin targeting π ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝒩 ​ ( v , 0 , I d ) \pi(x)\mathcal{N}(v;0,I_{d}) , where π ∝ e − ℰ \pi\propto e^{-\mathcal{E}} : [ d ​ X s d ​ V s ] = [ V s 0 ] ​ d ​ s ⏟ A + [ 0 − ∇ ℰ ​ ( X s ) ] ​ d ​ s ⏟ B + [ 0 − ζ ​ V s ​ d ​ s + 2 ​ ζ ​ d ​ B s ] ⏟ O , \displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{d}X_{s}\\ \mathrm{d}V_{s}\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}V_{s}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\mathrm{d}s}_{\mathrm{A}}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0\\ -\nabla\mathcal{E}(X_{s})\end{bmatrix}\mathrm{d}s}_{\mathrm{B}}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0\\ -\zeta V_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s+\sqrt{2\zeta}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathrm{O}}, (22) where ζ > 0 \zeta>0 is the friction coefficient and v ∈ ℝ d v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the auxiliary velocity variable. The underdamped Langevin dynamics is split into three parts: free transport of the position at fixed velocity (A), force-driven evolution of the velocity at fixed position (B), and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck evolution of the velocity, combining friction and Gaussian noise at fixed position (O). Their exact updates over a duration t ≥ 0 t\geq 0 are A t : \displaystyle\mathrm{A}_{t}:\quad ( x , v ) ⟼ ( x + t ​ v , v ) , \displaystyle(x,v)\longmapsto(x+tv,v), (23) B t : \displaystyle\mathrm{B}_{t}:\quad ( x , v ) ⟼ ( x , v − t ∇ ℰ ( x ) ) , \displaystyle(x,v)\longmapsto(x,v-t\nabla\mathcal{E}(x)), (24) O t : \displaystyle\mathrm{O}_{t}:\quad ( x , v ) ⟼ ( x , e − ζ ​ t ​ v + 1 − e − 2 ​ ζ ​ t ​ ξ ) , ξ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) . \displaystyle(x,v)\longmapsto\left(x,e^{-\zeta t}v+\sqrt{1-e^{-2\zeta t}}\,\xi\right),\qquad\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). (25) These exact substeps generally do not commute, so their composition provides a specific approximation of the full dynamics ( Leimkuhler and Matthews, 2013b , Section IV) . For example, the chronological order of a BAOAB step of size δ \delta is B δ / 2 ⟶ A δ / 2 ⟶ O δ ⟶ A δ / 2 ⟶ B δ / 2 . \mathrm{B}_{\delta/2}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{A}_{\delta/2}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{O}_{\delta}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{A}_{\delta/2}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{B}_{\delta/2}. (26) The letters specify the order of the updates; each repeated letter here uses a half step. Each update acts on the current state, with independent noise for each O substep. Symmetric Strang composition ( i.e. , letters forming a palindrome) give second-order weak accuracy under appropriate conditions ( Strang, 1968 ) .

sections.heading: HMC.
sections.text: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo introduces auxiliary momentum variables and uses Hamiltonian trajectories, with a correction for numerical integration error, to construct a target-invariant transition ( Neal, 2011 ) .

sections.heading: Stein variational gradient descent.
sections.text: Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) transports a set of interacting particles using a deterministic, kernel-based field ( Liu and Wang, 2016 ) . For a differentiable positive-definite kernel k k and step size δ > 0 \delta>0 , its update for particles { x i } i = 1 B \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B} is y i = x i + δ B ∑ j = 1 B [ − k ( x j , x i ) ∇ ℰ ( x j ) + ∇ x j k ( x j , x i ) ] , i = 1 , … , B . y_{i}=x_{i}+\frac{\delta}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B}\left[-k(x_{j},x_{i})\nabla\mathcal{E}(x_{j})+\nabla_{x_{j}}k(x_{j},x_{i})\right],\qquad i=1,\ldots,B. (27)

sections.heading: Multiple-step kernels.
sections.text: If K K is a π \pi -invariant kernel, so is K n K^{n} for n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 . Thus one can construct several-step kernels by iterating the primitive ones defined above, as we do in the experiments.

sections.heading: Acceptance-targeting step adaptation.
sections.text: We adapt the step size δ \delta of random-walk or Langevin MCMC during training to maintain a target acceptance rate α ⋆ \alpha^{\star} ( Andrieu and Thoms, 2008 ) . The update is log-space stochastic approximation, log ⁡ h t ← log ⁡ h t + η adapt ​ ( α ^ − α ⋆ ) , \log h_{t}\leftarrow\log h_{t}+\eta_{\mathrm{adapt}}(\hat{\alpha}-\alpha^{\star}), where α ^ \hat{\alpha} is the batch mean acceptance and h t ≔ δ β t h_{t}\coloneqq\frac{\delta}{\beta_{t}} is the temperature-rescaled step size. We then set the sampler’s step size to δ t = h t ​ β t \delta_{t}=h_{t}\beta_{t} and clip it to [ δ min , δ max ] [\delta_{\min},\delta_{\max}] .

sections.heading: C.2 Choice of divergence
sections.text: To compute the distance between two distributions, we rely on sample-based distribution metrics. In practice, these distances are computed using samples from both distributions.

sections.heading: Maximum mean discrepancy.
sections.text: One possible way to compute the distance between two distributions is use maximum mean discrepancy ( Gretton et al., 2012 , MMD;) . Given a positive definite kernel function, such as k ⁡ ( x , y ) = exp ⁡ ( − ‖ x − y ‖ h ) k(x,y)=\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-y\|}{h}\right) , where h h is a positive bandwidth and ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| is L 2 L_{2} distance, the MMD between two distributions μ 1 \mu_{1} and μ 2 \mu_{2} is defined as: MMD 2 ​ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) \displaystyle\text{MMD}^{2}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) ≔ 𝔼 x , x ′ ∼ μ 1 ​ [ k ⁡ ( x , x ′ ) ] + 𝔼 y , y ′ ∼ μ 2 ​ [ k ⁡ ( y , y ′ ) ] \displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim\mu_{1}}[k(x,x^{\prime})]+\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\mu_{2}}[k(y,y^{\prime})] − 2 ​ 𝔼 x ∼ μ 1 , y ∼ μ 2 ​ [ k ⁡ ( x , y ) ] , \displaystyle\phantom{=\;}-2\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{1},y\sim\mu_{2}}[k(x,y)], (28) which can be estimated by Monte Carlo sampling.

sections.heading: Squared 2-Wasserstein distance.
sections.text: For probability distributions μ 1 \mu_{1} and μ 2 \mu_{2} on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} with finite second moments, recall from ( 16 ) that the squared 2-Wasserstein distance is an optimal transport cost 𝒲 2 2 ​ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) ≔ inf γ ∈ Γ ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) ∫ ℝ d × ℝ d | x − y | 2 ​ 𝑑 γ ​ ( x , y ) , \displaystyle\mathcal{W}^{2}_{2}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})\coloneqq\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}|x-y|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y), (29) where Γ ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) \Gamma(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) contains joint distributions over ℝ d × ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} whose marginals are μ 1 \mu_{1} and μ 2 \mu_{2} .The 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} distance between empirical approximations to μ 1 \mu_{1} and μ 2 \mu_{2} is known as the minibatch 2-Wasserstein, and it converges to ( 29 ) as the number of samples increases ( Fatras et al., 2021 ) .

sections.heading: Sliced Wasserstein distance.
sections.text: The sliced Wasserstein distance ( Bonneel et al., 2015 ; Kolouri et al., 2019 ; Nadjahi et al., 2020 , SWD;) is a tractable surrogate that computes OT distances using 1 1 -dimensional projections. It is defined by 𝕊 2 2 ​ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) ≔ 𝔼 ω ​ [ 𝒲 2 2 ​ ( P ω ​ # ​ μ 1 , P ω ​ # ​ μ 2 ) ] , \mathbb{S}_{2}^{2}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\left[\mathcal{W}^{2}_{2}(P_{\omega\,\#}\mu_{1},P_{\omega\,\#}\mu_{2})\right], (30) where the expectation is taken over ω \omega uniform on the unit sphere in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . In practice, the expectation over the projection direction ω \omega is estimated with random projections. The quantity inside the expectation is a 1D OT distance between empirical distributions and is thus easily computed.

sections.heading: Sinkhorn divergence.
sections.text: Entropic regularisation is introduced to the transport problem ( 29 ) and provides a smoother optimisation problem that can be solved using Sinkhorn iterations. For regularisation strength ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , define ( Cuturi, 2013 ) OT ε ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) = inf γ ∈ Γ ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) [ ∫ | x − y | 2 d γ ( x , y ) + ε KL ( γ ∥ μ 1 ⊗ μ 2 ) ] . \operatorname{OT}_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})}\left[\int|x-y|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y)+\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}\left(\gamma\!\parallel\!\mu_{1}\otimes\mu_{2}\right)\right]. (31) The corresponding debiased Sinkhorn divergence subtracts the two self-interaction terms, S ε ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) = OT ε ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) − 1 2 ​ OT ε ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 1 ) − 1 2 ​ OT ε ⁡ ( μ 2 , μ 2 ) , \operatorname{S}_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})=\operatorname{OT}_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})-\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{OT}_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{1},\mu_{1})-\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{OT}_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{2},\mu_{2}), (32) so that S ε ⁡ ( μ , μ ) = 0 \operatorname{S}_{\varepsilon}(\mu,\mu)=0 . For empirical measures and the squared-Euclidean cost used here, S ε ⁡ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) \operatorname{S}_{\varepsilon}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) approaches 𝒲 2 2 ​ ( μ 1 , μ 2 ) \mathcal{W}^{2}_{2}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}) as ε ↓ 0 \varepsilon\downarrow 0 . As ε → ∞ \varepsilon\to\infty , it approaches the squared distance between the means of μ 1 \mu_{1} and μ 2 \mu_{2} , equivalently, the squared MMD associated with the linear kernel k ⁡ ( x , y ) = ⟨ x , y ⟩ k(x,y)=\langle x,y\rangle ( Feydy et al., 2019 , Section 1.2) .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We train OSIS and the baselines for five random seeds. After training, we draw five independent batches of 10,000 10{,}000 samples with different seeds at the selected checkpoint: the final training iteration for OSIS and the checkpoint with the highest ELBO for baselines, following Blessing et al. (2024) . Each sampler’s evaluation batch is compared with the same batch of 10,000 10{,}000 reference samples for all samplers. We average the results within each training seed, then report the mean and sample standard deviation across the five training-seed means. SMC uses five repetition groups instead of training seeds. The reference rows provide a floor on each metric by comparing two independent target batches of samples. We report empirical 𝒲 2 2 \mathcal{W}_{2}^{2} with unnormalised squared Euclidean cost, computed using POT ( Flamary et al., 2021 ) with convergence checks. MMD corresponds to the square root of the biased Gaussian kernel MMD-squared estimate, with bandwidth fixed per target to the median pairwise distance in an independent 10,000 10{,}000 -sample batch from the target distribution.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We retrain FAB ( Midgley et al., 2023 ) , PIS ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ) , and DIS ( Berner et al., 2024 ) , and run SMC ( Del Moral et al., 2006 ) using the reference implementation of Blessing et al. (2024) . FAB uses an 8-layer Real-NVP flow with [ 64 , 64 ] [64,64] conditioner MLPs, 12 intermediate distributions, 10 HMC transitions per intermediate distribution, a replay buffer, and α \alpha -divergence loss with α = 2 \alpha=2 . It trains for 3,000 iterations with four replay updates per iteration, at batch size 2,000 (1,000 for both NICE targets). PIS and DIS use the PISGRADNet with width-64 MLPs and Fourier time features, trained for 40,000 updates with a batch size of 2,000 and 128 integration steps. For other hyperparameters, we use those reported in Blessing et al. (2024) . For ManyWell d = 32 , 64 d=32,64 and 40GMM d = 10 d=10 , since the paper does not provide default hyperparameters, we performed a grid search over the key hyperparameters, as provided in Table 5 , and selected the one with the best ELBO. SMC uses 2,000 particles, 10 HMC transitions per annealing interval, and resampling threshold of 0.3 0.3 . It uses 256 temperatures for GMM-10D and ManyWell (dimension 32 32 and 64 64 ) targets, and 128 otherwise. For TB + + MALA ( Sendera et al., 2024 ) and SubTB + + SMC ( Choi et al., 2026 ) , we use the original implementation of Choi et al. (2026) and reimplement TB + + MALA within the same codebase to simplify benchmarking. While the reimplemented TB + + MALA is not identical to the original from Sendera et al. (2024) , we ensure that the algorithm performs at least as well as, or better than, the original on synthetic targets. For these two baselines, we set the network architectures and common hyperparameters (learning rate and initial std.) to match those of DIS, while fixing algorithm-specific hyperparameters as reported in the original papers. sections.heading: Model architecture for G θ G_{\theta} .
sections.text: In all our experiments we use a ResNet architecture with MLP layers. The inputs are first projected to a 256 256 -dimensional latent, then follow 3 residual blocks of the form x ↦ x + SiLU ⁡ ( W ​ x + b ) , W ∈ ℝ 256 × 256 x\mapsto x+\mathrm{SiLU}(Wx+b),\,W\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times 256} , then the outputs are projected to the output dimension.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: We train OSIS with 1200 1200 outer steps and 50 50 inner steps, following the procedure presented in Algorithm 3 . We use an empirical approximation of OT loss ( Section C.2 ) and use MALA with adaptive step size ( Section C.1 ) as the MCMC algorithm, which we run for 20 20 steps. For the initial 1000 1000 outer iterations we train the algorithm on a tempered target, the temperature follows a cosine schedule with initial temperature 2.0 2.0 and final temperature 1.0 1.0 . Next, we train OSIS for 200 200 more iterations keeping the temperature fixed at 1.0 1.0 . We use the AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) optimiser with learning rate 0.001 0.001 and no weight decay.

sections.heading: E.3 Drift parameterisation of OSIS
sections.text: We evaluate whether OSIS can benefit from a drift-based regression formulation motivated by Wasserstein gradient flows. This formulation expresses the generator update as a regression task towards samples displaced by an estimated drift field, with the regression targets held fixed during differentiation. For OT-based objectives, computing these targets still requires the corresponding transport information. The drift parameterisation yields lower mean values for both metrics on ManyWell ( d = 32 d=32 ). On 40GMM ( d = 2 d=2 ), both mean Sinkhorn divergence and mean MMD are higher, although the differences are within the scale of the reported variability. Whitammer Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning Affiliation: CIFAR Fellow * Equal contribution Abstract Efficient sampling from Bayesian posterior distributions in high dimensions remains a hard problem, despite advances in theory and algorithms. Multiple steps are usually required to draw unbiased samples, for example, iterations of an MCMC algorithm or integration steps in a diffusion-based amortised sampler. However, scalable one-step amortised inference remains a challenging open problem. In this work, we build upon recent progress in data-driven generative modelling to offer a possible solution for one-step amortised sampling. Our one-step implicit sampler ( OSIS ) uses short-time MCMC dynamics to define a local target for the evolution of an implicitly modelled distribution. In the asymptotic limit, the modelled distribution is a fixed point of the MCMC kernel and thus samples from the target. We analyse the convergence properties of OSIS and show connections with other generative modelling and sampling algorithms. We study various design choices and show that OSIS performs well compared to multi-step amortised samplers and non-amortised MCMC baselines while being far more efficient at sampling time. * * footnotetext: Correspondence to vincent.paulinef@gmail.com and kirill.tamogashev@ed.ac.uk . 1 Introduction The sampling problem. Many problems in physics, biology, statistics, and machine learning ( Welling and Teh, 2011 ; Wirnsberger et al., 2020 ; Noé et al., 2019 ; Holdijk et al., 2023 ) require drawing samples from a distribution whose density is known up to a normalising constant. Formally, this means sampling from a distribution defined via an energy function ℰ : ℝ d → ℝ \mathcal{E}:\mathbb{R}^{d}	o\mathbb{R} , with density π ⁡ ( x ) = e − ℰ ⁡ ( x ) / Z , Z = ∫ ℝ d e − ℰ ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x . \pi(x)={e^{-\mathcal{E}(x)}}/Z,\quad Z={\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\mathcal{E}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x}. (1) A typical instance of this problem is Bayesian inference: a posterior π ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) ∝ p ⁡ ( x ) ​ p ​ ( y ∣ x ) \pi(x\mid y)\propto p(x)p(y\mid x) over a variable x x given an observation y y has the form in ( 1 ) with ℰ ⁡ ( x ) = − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( x ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) \mathcal{E}(x)=-\log p(x)-\log p(y\mid x) . The classic way to sample from a distribution as in ( 1 ) is by using (training-free) Monte Carlo algorithms. Many such algorithms draw samples by simulating an ergodic chain using π \pi -invariant kernels for a sufficiently long time. Popular Monte Carlo algorithms include Metropolis-Hastings ( Metropolis et al., 1953 ; Hastings, 1970 ) , unadjusted and Metropolis-adjusted Langevin ( Rossky et al., 1978 ; Besag, 1994 ; Roberts and Tweedie, 1996 ) , Hamiltonian Monte Carlo ( Duane et al., 1987 ; Neal, 2011 ) , and sequential Monte Carlo ( Del Moral et al., 2006 ) . The use of these methods comes at the cost of running chains for many steps, or with many simulated particles, to obtain high-quality samples from the target. Generative modelling algorithms that learn to imitate unbiased samples from a distribution – i.e. , approximate an empirical measure – scale quite successfully, as evidenced by many large-scale applications of deep learning ( Kong et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) . Meanwhile, generative modelling algorithms that rely only on a density function, without unbiased samples, continue to lag behind, and scaling them remains a challenge despite the deep significance of this problem. Amortised sampling. Deep learning has brought about new possibilities for introducing learnable components into sampling algorithms. Such components allow to spend more time and compute for training, yet gain speed when sampling and exploit generalisable structure in the target. Amortisation techniques include learning MCMC transition kernels ( Song et al., 2017 ; Samsonov et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , amortising MCMC dynamics ( Li et al., 2017 ) , and training density estimators to sample from unnormalised distributions ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Midgley et al., 2023 ) . The most successful family of amortised samplers adopts diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) as approximators of the target distribution ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ; Richter et al., 2024 ; Sendera et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2025 ; Berner et al., 2026 ; Havens et al., 2025 , e.g. ,) . Diffusion samplers introduce a learnable stochastic process to model the transition dynamics from a known distribution to a target, usually by approximately reversing a fixed noising process. In contrast to diffusion models trained using a variational bound on the likelihood of empirical samples, diffusion samplers are trained using stochastic optimal control objectives ( Zhang and Chen, 2022 ; Berner et al., 2024 ) or path-space divergences ( Richter et al., 2020 ; Lahlou et al., 2023 ) , among other choices. Recent work has found and exploited connections between diffusion samplers and amortisation of SMC ( Choi et al., 2026 ) . Although diffusion samplers allow for a considerable inference speed-up by avoiding long-chain MCMC, they require simulation of a neural stochastic dynamical system during both training and sampling. Amortised sampling with a single neural function evaluation, however, remains a challenge. Although it is possible to use normalising flows for one-step sampling ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ) , they require the invertibility of a neural network and efficient computation of its Jacobian, both of which remain significant constraints. More recent work shows that such methods scale poorly and are prone to mode collapse ( He et al., 2025 ) . These methods can further be placed within a Monte Carlo outer loop and augmented with MCMC sampling ( Midgley et al., 2023 ) . In an attempt to design an efficient one-step sampler, we take a different approach, drawing inspiration from the novel paradigm in generative modelling termed drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ) . Drifting models evolve a implicit distribution towards an empirical target by defining a local direction for its evolution via a drifting field estimated from batches of target and generated samples. Such an approach, cannot be directly applied to sampling, as it requires access to samples from the target distribution to compute the drifting field. Our contributions. We bypass this limitation by using an MCMC kernel invariant to the target distribution to implicitly define a drifting field. This leads us to the first main contribution: (1) We propose an algorithm for training a one-step implicit sampler ( OSIS ) using an objective that enforces invariance of the sampler’s output distribution to a target-invariant MCMC kernel ( Section 2.1 ). There have been prior attempts to design a one-step amortised sampling algorithm, using kernel density approximations to circumvent data unavailability ( Cao et al., 2026 ) and using adversarial training ( Li et al., 2017 ) . We discuss the connections between OSIS , drifting models, computational Wasserstein gradient flows, and this prior work in Section 3 . We also study the theoretical properties of OSIS , showing global convergence under assumptions similar to those in the MCMC literature: 1. We prove convergence of OSIS under asymptotic conditions and constraints on the target ( Section 4 ). To achieve scalability and efficiency in practice, we study the empirical performance of OSIS under different design choices, such as choice of MCMC kernel, empirical divergence, and other techniques: 1. We study design choices for OSIS ( § 5 ) and their influence on performance ( Table 3 ). Finally, we benchmark our sampler on amortised inference problems ranging from synthetic targets to posterior sampling under large-scale image model priors, leading to our final contribution: 1. The connection between generative modelling and implicit models, those without a parametrisation of density, goes back to Mohamed and Lakshminarayanan (2016) . Subsequent works explored algorithms that use MCMC to train implicit samplers: Feng et al. (2017) amortises Stein variational gradient descent ( Liu and Wang, 2016 , SVGD;) , while Titsias (2017) fits an invertible map to sample from the distribution induced by a short MCMC chain. Related approaches include Hoffman (2017) , Ruiz and Titsias (2019) , Gabrié et al. (2022) , and Yi and Liu (2023) . The closest precursor to OSIS is Li et al. (2017) . That algorithm initialises an MCMC chain from an implicit approximation network, applies a transition kernel, and updates the network with an adversarial loss matching the initial samples to their few-step refinements. OSIS differs from this line of work in three key ways. First, unlike Li et al. (2017) , OSIS does not rely on an adversarial loss, but remains stable with a fixed choice of empirical divergence. Second, OSIS is compatible with any MCMC kernel and any divergence between distributions, and we compare several choices of each (see Table 3 for kernels and Tables 1 and 1 for divergences). Third, we link the convergence of these methods to the convergence of the underlying MCMC kernel and establish a connection to Wasserstein gradient flows that was not known before in the sampling context (see Section 4 ). Connection to drifting models. OSIS can be linked to drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , which define a local target for the evolution of a modelled distribution to guide it towards a target given empirically through data samples. Although OSIS and drifting models solve different problems (approximating an empirical data distribution and an energy-based distribution, respectively), they share some similarities. In Deng et al. (2026) , stationarity of an implicitly defined generative model is expressed through a drifting field, a vector field defining an evolution of particles under which the target distribution is stationary under asymptotic conditions. The field is defined similarly to the gradient of a kernel-based divergence and thus evolves model-generated samples towards the data distribution over the course of training. Unlike in diffusion and flow-based models, which approximate a time-dependent evolution, this field is a non-stationary training target, rather than part of the generation process. More recent works propose other ways to define this drifting field, some of which can be identified with gradients of divergences between distributions, making the training process simulate a gradient flow ( He et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . As we discuss below, OSIS shares parts of this connection; however, drifting models and their successors approximate the vector field giving the gradient flow , whereas OSIS uses the vector field giving the gradient flow to define the local target for optimisation . Cao et al. (2026) propose several ways to adapt drifting models for sampling. Their method relies on either Monte Carlo simulation or second-order derivatives to approximate the gradient of the energy, both of which scale poorly with dimensionality. In contrast, OSIS defines the drift implicitly by computing the divergence between two probability distributions. Connection to computational Wasserstein gradient flows.
